name: Practice Test 9
description: Full-length SAT Reading & Writing · 2 modules × 27 = 54 questions.

questions.passage: Skeptics had predicted that opening the sealed archive would transform the field. A decade on, the effect has proved ______: the handful of dissertations that draw on the new documents have gone almost entirely uncited.

questions.passage: The received view treats the guild's secrecy as ordinary economic self-interest: a cartel guarding its techniques. The evidence for that motive, though, is entirely circumstantial—no guild document states it—and the same secrecy is equally consistent with a rival account in which the mystery was the product, the buyers paying not for a better blade but for the assurance that its making could not be reproduced. This essay does not adjudicate between the two accounts. It argues, more narrowly, that the economic reading has prevailed less because the evidence favors it than because it flatters a discipline that likes its motives legible.
questions.question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To establish, on the basis of surviving guild documents, that the guild's secrecy was intended to protect a commercial monopoly.
To adjudicate between the economic account of the guild's secrecy and the rival account in which the secrecy was itself the product being sold.
To trace the history of the metalworking techniques that the guild guarded and to explain why outsiders were unable to reproduce them.
To argue that the economic explanation of the guild's secrecy has prevailed for reasons of disciplinary preference rather than evidential support.

questions.passage: That the medieval warm period was global has become a talking point, invoked to suggest that present-day warming is nothing new. The inference runs from a set of European chronicles and North Atlantic ice cores to a claim about the entire planet. But the same centuries, read in tree rings from the southern Andes and in corals from the tropical Pacific, show no synchronized warmth at all—some regions warming, others cooling, the timing scattered across two hundred years. What had looked global, it turns out, was the reach of the records, not the reach of the warmth.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It describes a past climatic period, surveys the competing methods used to reconstruct it, and recommends that tree-ring data be preferred to ice-core data.
It presents an inference drawn from a geographically limited body of evidence, introduces evidence from other regions that fails to confirm it, and then locates the error in the original inference.
It states a scientific consensus, presents an anomaly that the consensus cannot explain, and predicts that the consensus will shortly be overturned.
It contrasts the medieval warm period with present-day warming and argues that the two have fundamentally different underlying causes.

questions.passage: Museums increasingly display their looted holdings alongside frank labels detailing exactly how each object was taken. The candor is real; and yet it quietly performs a second function, converting the museum from the beneficiary of a theft into the honest narrator of one, and letting the object remain precisely where the theft delivered it. Transparency about a wrong, on this account, can become one of the ways in which the wrong is preserved.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It offers evidence that museums have, in recent years, begun returning their looted objects to the communities from which those objects were originally taken.

It grants the sincerity of the museums' disclosures while contending that those disclosures also work to legitimize the museums' continued possession of the objects, a paradox that the final sentence generalizes.
It concedes a criticism of the museums' new labeling practices that the final sentence then goes on to rebut.
It explains the sequence of historical events by which the looted objects first came to enter the museums' permanent collections.

questions.passage: He had never stolen, and he was proud of it, in the way a man is proud of a thing that has cost him something. What it had cost him he could not have said until this evening; and then, going over the great ledgers by lamplight as he had gone over them ten thousand times, he understood that the merchant's trust had not been a tribute to his honesty but the occasion of it—that a man watched as closely as the other clerks were watched would never have had, in all those years, the one thing Ludvik had been given without asking and had never learned to value: the chance, entirely his own and observed by no one, to be either honest or not.
questions.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Ludvik comes to see that the honesty he has prized was made possible only by a trust that never once tested it, and so was never quite the achievement he had taken it to be.
Ludvik is tormented by the memory of a theft that he committed early in his career and has managed to conceal for twenty years.
Ludvik resolves to confront the merchant at last about the inadequate wages he has been paid over two decades of loyal service.
Ludvik concludes that the merchant's long trust in him was misplaced and that he has never genuinely deserved it.

questions.passage: The Devil's Hole pupfish lives in a single limestone pool in the Nevada desert, the smallest range of any vertebrate on Earth. The pool opens onto an aquifer whose level the fish track with peculiar exactness: their one spawning shelf sits just below the waterline, and a drop of only a few centimeters exposes it to the air, ending reproduction for the season. Because that aquifer is drawn on by farms many kilometers away, the fish's survival hangs on pumping it has no way of sensing and on a shelf whose usefulness a single dry year can cancel.
questions.question: According to the text, what is the effect of a drop of a few centimeters in the pool's water level?
options: It causes the fish to migrate to a deeper portion of the connected aquifer until the level recovers.
It prompts the distant farms to reduce the amount of water that they draw from the aquifer.
It exposes the fish's only spawning shelf to the air and thereby halts the fish's reproduction for that season.
It severs the pool's connection to the aquifer that ordinarily protects the fish from change.

questions.passage: A historian of technology argues that the spread of the mechanical clock owed little to any demand for accurate timekeeping and much to the bell: monasteries already rang the canonical hours by hand, and the clock's first decisive advantage was simply that it could trip a bell on schedule with no one awake to pull the rope.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the historian's argument?
options: The earliest mechanical clocks had neither dials nor hands and could not display the time at all; they were built for the sole purpose of striking a bell at fixed intervals.
Mechanical clocks grew substantially more accurate over the two centuries that followed their first appearance in European monasteries.
A number of monasteries went on paying a person to ring the hours by hand for decades after mechanical clocks had become available to them.
The mechanical clock was among the most intricate machines that were produced anywhere in medieval Europe during the period.

questions.passage: Observing that the countries which export the most tend also to have the fastest-growing economies, an analyst concluded that raising a country's exports causes its economy to grow more quickly.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most seriously weaken the analyst's conclusion?
options: A few of the countries with the fastest-growing economies exported goods that had been manufactured largely out of imported components.
The countries in the study varied widely in their populations, their land areas, and the particular mix of goods that they exported.
Among the countries studied, a surge in exports typically followed, rather than preceded, the domestic investment and productivity gains that were independently driving the faster growth.
Export figures for several of the countries had been compiled using methods that differed in minor respects from one country to the next.

questions.question: Which choice best uses data from the table to support the board's observation?
options: Cinta drew 800 visitors for each object it displayed—the most of the four museums—yet Delft, not Cinta, drew the highest total attendance.
Delft both displayed the most objects and occupied the largest floor area of the four museums in the study.
Aldan drew more visitors for each object it displayed than Brno did, but fewer than Cinta did.

questions.passage: A team gave chess novices a memory test: shown a position from a real game for five seconds and then asked to reconstruct it, the novices placed only a handful of pieces correctly, while masters placed nearly all of them. The masters' advantage vanished, however, when the same pieces were scattered at random across the board rather than taken from a real game; on random boards, masters did no better than novices. The result indicates that the masters' superior recall depends on ______
questions.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: a general capacity for visual memory that exceeds the novices' across every kind of material equally.
the additional time that the masters, unlike the novices, were permitted to study the board before reconstructing it.
their ability to encode a position in terms of the familiar, meaningful patterns that a random arrangement does not contain.
their having previously memorized the specific games from which the test positions had been drawn.

questions.passage: Two neighboring towns levied the same new tax on sugary drinks, but only one paired the tax with a prominent public campaign explaining where the revenue would go. In the town with the campaign, consumption fell 14 percent and public support for the tax rose over the following year. In the town without it, consumption fell an almost identical 13 percent—but support for the tax dropped sharply, and it was repealed by referendum within two years. Taken together, the results suggest that the campaign's main effect was ______
questions.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: to reduce sugary-drink consumption by a substantially greater amount than the tax on its own could have achieved.
not on how much residents drank, which the tax alone proved enough to change, but on whether they would tolerate the tax long enough for that change to endure.
to raise a larger sum of public revenue than the same tax generated in the neighboring town that lacked a campaign.
to persuade the town's residents that the new tax would have no effect on the retail price of sugary drinks.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • Two desalination plants opened on the same coast in 2023.
  • Plant A uses reverse osmosis; it produces 90 million liters a day and uses 3.5 kWh per 1,000 liters.
  • Plant B uses thermal distillation; it produces 90 million liters a day and uses 10 kWh per 1,000 liters.
  • Both plants draw from the same seawater intake.
questions.question: The student wants to emphasize the difference in the two plants' energy use. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Plant A, which uses reverse osmosis, and Plant B, which uses thermal distillation, both opened along the same stretch of coast during the year 2023.

Although Plant A and Plant B each produce 90 million liters of fresh water a day from the same seawater intake, Plant B's thermal distillation uses 10 kWh per 1,000 liters—nearly three times the 3.5 kWh that Plant A's reverse osmosis requires.
Plant B relies on thermal distillation and consumes 10 kWh for every 1,000 liters of the fresh water that it produces each day.
Both Plant A and Plant B draw all of the seawater that they process from exactly the same coastal intake on that shore.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • “Moral hazard” is the tendency of being protected from a risk to make a person take on more of it.
  • A driver with excellent insurance may, without meaning to, drive less carefully.
  • The insurer, not the driver, bears the financial cost of a crash.
  • So the protection can increase the very behavior it insures against.
  • Insurers use deductibles partly to counter this tendency.
questions.question: The student wants to explain moral hazard to an audience unfamiliar with the term. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: An insurer, rather than the driver whom it insures, is the party that bears the financial cost of an accident that the driver has while covered by a policy.
Insurers make use of deductibles in part because doing so allows them to counteract the effects that moral hazard would otherwise have on the people they insure.

Moral hazard is the tendency of protection from a risk to make people take on more of it: a driver with excellent insurance, knowing that the insurer rather than he will bear the cost of a crash, may drive less carefully, so that the protection ends up increasing the very behavior it insures against.
Moral hazard is the tendency of being protected from some particular risk to lead a person to take on a greater amount of that very risk than before.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • The researcher Nils Auer hypothesized that, among bird species, those that store food for winter tend to have a larger hippocampus (a brain region used in spatial memory) relative to body size.
  • Species G stores food heavily; its relative hippocampus index is 84.
  • Species H does not store food; its index is 29.
  • Species I stores food moderately; its index is 55.
questions.question: The student wants to use the data to support Auer's hypothesis. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: The species that stores food most heavily, G, had the largest hippocampus relative to body size (index 84), while the non-storing species, H, had the smallest (index 29), and the moderate storer, I, fell between the two.
Species I, which stores food for winter to a moderate degree, has a relative hippocampus index of 55.
All three of the bird species examined possess a hippocampus whose size can be measured relative to the body.
Species G stores more food for the winter than either Species H or Species I does.

questions.passage: A familiar objection to the electoral college is that it can seat a president whom most voters opposed. The objection is sound as far as it goes, but pressing it is not my concern here. My interest is in a subtler cost, one that survives even in the elections the college gets “right”: because a mere handful of states decide the outcome, the whole machinery of persuasion—money, attention, promises—flows toward them and their particular grievances, so that the system does not merely risk installing the wrong winner but reliably distorts what any winner, right or wrong, is induced to care about.
questions.question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To press the familiar objection that the electoral college can seat a president whom a majority of the voters actively opposed.
To set aside the usual objection to the electoral college in order to argue that the system distorts candidates' priorities even when it produces the majority's preferred winner.
To propose a specific reform that would prevent the electoral college from ever seating the loser of the national popular vote.
To compare the American electoral college with the various systems that other democracies use to elect their leaders.

questions.passage: The extinction is usually told as a morality play: humans arrive, humans hunt, the great flightless birds fall. The chronology was always the play's weak point, and new dating has now broken it outright. On three separate islands the birds vanish not when the first people land but between six hundred and nine hundred years afterward—long enough for hunting to have finished them many times over, but long enough, too, for the rats and pigs that had come ashore in the same canoes to have eaten every egg in every nest. The people, it seems, were present at the extinction without being its agents; their livestock were the killers, and the play has been prosecuting the wrong defendant.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It lays out a standard explanation, presents new evidence about timing that the explanation cannot accommodate, and then offers a revised account that reassigns the cause.
It narrates a sequence of island extinctions and ranks the islands according to how rapidly the birds on each of them disappeared.
It defends the standard explanation of the extinction against a recent challenge founded on new radiocarbon dating.
It weighs two long-established theories of the extinction and concludes that the available evidence cannot decide between them.

questions.passage: For a century the temple's precise alignment to the solstice sunrise was cited as proof of its builders' astronomical sophistication. But any building with four sides aligns to something, and a culture that watched the sky as closely as this one did would surely have noticed the coincidence and, finding it auspicious, told a story that made the alignment deliberate—so that a myth of intention is exactly what we should expect to find whether the intention was real or not. The alignment, in short, can no longer do the work that the old argument asked of it.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It supplies additional astronomical evidence confirming that the temple's builders did align the structure to the solstice on purpose.
It concedes that the temple's alignment was a coincidence but maintains that the builders' sophistication is established by other means entirely.

It undermines the inference drawn in the first sentence by showing that the evidence for deliberate design would be present even if the design were accidental, a conclusion the final sentence states outright.
It explains the specific surveying method by which the temple's builders would have fixed the direction of the solstice sunrise.

questions.passage: The girl was doing everything wrong, and everything right. She hurried the pause that Marte had once made the whole house wait through; she threw away the line that Marte had built an entire act around; and the effect, which by every law Marte knew should have been ruin, was somehow more alive than Marte's own had ever been. Marte understood, watching, that the pause and the emphasis had not been the play's genius but hers—her own solution to a problem the play had set her—and that the girl had simply not inherited the problem, and so had been free to discover that it was not, after all, there.
questions.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Marte is dismayed to watch a promising young performer ruin a great role through sheer inexperience and a disregard for its established interpretation.
Marte concludes that the younger actress has carefully studied, and meaningfully improved upon, the interpretation that first made Marte famous.
Marte comes to regret having devoted thirty years of her career to a role that she now believes never truly suited her particular gifts.
Watching the younger actress succeed by discarding her signature choices, Marte realizes that those choices had solved a problem peculiar to herself rather than one belonging to the play.

questions.passage: The Turritopsis jellyfish has been called immortal, and the label is not quite hyperbole. Injured or starving, an adult does not die but reverses its own development, its cells transforming into a juvenile polyp that will, in time, bud off new adults genetically identical to the first. The reversal can in principle repeat without limit. In practice, though, almost every individual is eaten or infected long before it can perform the trick, so that a creature theoretically exempt from aging remains, in the open ocean, as mortal as anything else.
questions.question: According to the text, what does an adult Turritopsis do when it is injured or starving?
options: It reverses its development into a juvenile polyp, which in time buds off new adults that are genetically identical to the first.
It produces a batch of eggs that develop directly into juveniles genetically identical to itself.
It reverses its development in order to avoid being eaten or infected by other ocean creatures.
It performs a reversal of its development that, once carried out, cannot afterward be repeated.

questions.passage: An architectural historian argues that the cathedral's celebrated height was not an end its builders pursued for its own sake but a byproduct of acoustics: the plainchant sung there acquired its otherworldly resonance only in a very tall, narrow vessel, and the builders, she contends, simply raised the roof until the sound was right.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the historian's argument?
options: The cathedral was, at the time of its completion, the tallest enclosed space that had yet been constructed anywhere in Europe.
Plainchant of the kind sung in the cathedral was also performed in a great many other churches across the same region during the period.
The cathedral's remarkable height has been admired by visitors and imitated by later builders for many centuries since its completion.
Surviving building accounts record that work on the nave was halted for two years while the choir tested the resonance at successive heights, resuming each time only once the singers had approved.

questions.passage: A study found that students who took handwritten notes scored higher on a later test than students who typed their notes, and the authors concluded that writing notes by hand causes better retention of the material.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most seriously weaken the authors' conclusion?
options: The students who typed their notes reported that they had found it easier and less tiring to keep pace with the lecturer than the students who wrote by hand did.
The test used in the study emphasized conceptual understanding of the material rather than the recall of specific facts and figures.

The students chose for themselves whether to handwrite or to type, and those who chose to handwrite were, on entering the study, already the stronger test-takers by a margin that fully accounts for the later gap.
A small number of the students who took handwritten notes later transcribed those notes into a computer before sitting the test.

questions.passage: In an experiment, readers evaluated a job applicant from a written file. Half the files described the applicant as “persistent”; the other half, otherwise identical, described the same applicant as “stubborn.” Readers rated the “persistent” applicant as both more competent and more likable, even though the behavior described—refusing to drop a proposal after three rejections—was word for word the same in the two versions. The finding suggests that the readers' judgments were shaped less by the applicant's actual conduct than by ______
questions.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: the evaluative coloring carried by the single word chosen to label conduct that was in every other respect described identically.
the number of times the applicant's proposal had been rejected before it was ultimately accepted.
the readers' own prior convictions about what it is that makes a job applicant genuinely competent.
the differing length and level of detail of the written files that the readers were given to evaluate.

questions.passage: Hoping to curb prescribing of a costly drug, a hospital began showing each physician, on the prescribing screen, how his own rate compared with that of his peers. Prescribing of the drug fell 18 percent. But prescribing of a second drug in the same class—one the intervention never displayed and never mentioned—fell almost as much, 15 percent, over the same period, though no comparison for it was ever shown to anyone. Taken together, the results suggest that what altered the physicians' behavior was ______
questions.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: the physicians' discovery that the second drug was, in fact, just as costly to the hospital as the first.
not the specific comparison they were shown, but their new awareness that their prescribing was being watched at all.
the growing strength of the evidence that the first drug was less effective than the alternatives to it.
a shortage of the first drug that happened to coincide with the beginning of the hospital's intervention.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • Two libraries replaced their lighting in 2023.
  • Library P installed LED fixtures; the project cost $400,000 and cut annual energy use by 620,000 kWh.
  • Library Q installed skylights and daylight sensors; the project cost $1,300,000 and cut annual energy use by 640,000 kWh.
  • Both libraries occupy about the same floor area.
questions.question: The student wants to emphasize the difference in what the two projects cost. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • “Regression to the mean” is the tendency of an unusually extreme measurement to be followed by one closer to the average.

  • That drop does not mean she has actually gotten worse.
  • Part of any extreme score is owed to luck, which does not repeat.

questions.question: The student wants to explain regression to the mean to an audience unfamiliar with the term. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: A student who scores far above her usual level on some particular test will tend to score at least somewhat lower on the next test that she takes.
Mistaking an instance of regression to the mean for a genuine change in a person's underlying ability is an error that people commit fairly often.
Regression to the mean is the tendency of a measurement that is extreme to be followed, in turn, by another measurement that lies closer to the average.

Regression to the mean is the tendency of an unusually extreme measurement to be followed by one nearer the average: a student who scores far above her usual level tends to score lower next time not because she has gotten worse but because part of any extreme score is luck, which does not repeat—and mistaking that ordinary fall-back for a real change is a common error.
